outputs.L1:
In September 1607, the village of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by an unidentified disease that claimed the lives of all its inhabitants. The village was subsequently razed, and its official records were expunged.

In 2007, an account written by the local undertaker was discovered buried among the roots of a tree in the square of the quarantined village, revealing details of the disaster:

They sent a horse along the roads to warn that our town had been sealed within; its bloodied hooves had been left unshod. The shoes were kept, either to preserve the iron or to bless the fate of those who remained beyond the glens or down along the coast.

The horse’s message reached us while sentries held their posts. A note was tied around its neck, declaring that death would soon arrive, bringing its fevered knock to every door: the butcher’s shop, the mill, the church.

The sternest men of the village put on brave faces until the store of ale ran dry. The women covered their mouths with cloth and held their husbands as they died.

The disease took hold with sudden force. We believed we might silence the moans, and so we skinned and burned the failing horse, letting the fire consume its bones.

My children’s skin turned cold and flushed. Acquainted as I was with death, I recognized their end and held their trust; so I cut their throats and drew in their final breath.

I dug their graves, and then dug more.

In September of 1607, the settlement of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by a mysterious illness that killed every person living there. Afterward, the village was burned to the ground, and its official documentation was erased. In 2007, a written account by the village undertaker was discovered beneath the roots of a tree in the square of the quarantined settlement, revealing the events of the catastrophe.

A horse had been sent down the roads to warn others that our town had been sealed off. Its hooves were bloody, and its shoes had been removed. The iron was either being saved for use elsewhere or kept as a charm for those who remained beyond the valleys or along the coast. The animal reached us while the guards stood watch, carrying a note fastened to its neck. The message announced that death was approaching and that its fever would soon visit every place: the butcher’s stall, the mill, and the church alike.

Even the strongest men in the village tried to appear fearless, but their courage lasted only until the ale was gone. The women covered their mouths with cloth and clung to their husbands while they died. The sickness spread with terrifying speed. Believing we might silence the suffering, we flayed the exhausted horse and burned it, leaving the flames to devour its bones.

My children grew chilled and fever-bright. Since death was familiar to me, I recognized what was coming. Knowing their fate, and holding their faith in me, I ended their lives by cutting their throats and drawing in their final breath. I buried them, and then I dug still more graves.
outputs.L3:
In September 1607, the isolated village of Fianaise Bhréagach was overtaken by a mysterious and devastating disease. The illness appeared without warning and spread with terrifying speed, moving from household to household until no family was left untouched. Within a short time, every inhabitant of the village was dead.

In the aftermath, the authorities took extreme measures. Fianaise Bhréagach was burned to the ground, and its official records were deliberately erased. Parish documents, burial registers, land records, and written references to the village were destroyed or removed, as though the settlement had never existed. For centuries, only fragments of rumor survived: stories of a cursed place, a sealed road, and a village whose name was not to be spoken.

In 2007, however, a buried account was discovered that brought the story of Fianaise Bhréagach back into the light. The account had been written by an undertaker who had lived through the village’s final days and hidden his testimony before his own death. His record described the outbreak in grim detail, offering the first clear evidence of what had happened there in September 1607.

According to the undertaker’s account, the first sign of disaster came with the arrival of a horse. It was unshod, bloodied, and half-mad with exhaustion, stumbling into the village without a rider. Fastened to it was a warning: the town had been placed under quarantine, and death was near. Whether the message came from nearby officials, fleeing travelers, or someone who had already witnessed the disease elsewhere was unclear. But by the time the warning reached Fianaise Bhréagach, it was already too late.

The sickness spread rapidly. The undertaker described fever, delirium, and sudden death. Families locked themselves indoors, only to perish together. Neighbors stopped answering doors. The church bell rang until there was no one left strong enough to pull the rope. As the dead accumulated faster than they could be buried, fear overtook the survivors. Some abandoned their loved ones in the hope of saving themselves. Others turned violent, convinced that infection, witchcraft, or divine punishment had entered their homes.

In the village’s final days, desperation gave way to horror. Parents buried children with their own hands. The sick were left outside in the cold. Some families, trapped between grief and terror, committed acts that the undertaker could barely bring himself to describe. His account suggests that the disease did not merely destroy the bodies of the villagers; it broke the bonds that had held the community together.

By the time outside forces returned, Fianaise Bhréagach was silent. The decision was made to burn what remained and erase the village from record, perhaps to prevent panic, perhaps to hide the scale of the failure, or perhaps because those who found it believed the place itself had become dangerous. For four hundred years, the village existed only as a vanished name. The undertaker’s buried testimony remains the only surviving witness to its last days, preserving the memory of a community consumed by sickness, fear, and the certainty that death was coming.

In 2007, during a survey of an abandoned burial ground in the west of Ireland, archaeologists uncovered a sealed pit beneath the collapsed foundation of what had once been a mortuary shed. Inside it lay the remains of a man, buried alone and hastily, with a leather satchel wrapped against his ribs. The satchel had almost entirely rotted away, but within it were fragments of parchment, preserved by the cold, wet soil and the clay that had sealed the grave. After months of conservation, the writing was identified as the account of an undertaker who had served the village of Fianaise Bhréagach during a devastating plague in 1607.

No official record of the village’s destruction had survived. Parish registers from the surrounding district were missing for that year, tax rolls had been amended, and later maps showed only blank pasture where Fianaise Bhréagach had stood. Local tradition spoke vaguely of “the forbidden valley” and of a bell that rang until no hand remained to pull it, but these stories had long been dismissed as folklore. The undertaker’s account changed that. It provided the first direct testimony of a catastrophe that appears to have been deliberately erased from public memory.

According to the manuscript, the sickness arrived in early spring. At first it was mistaken for an ordinary fever. A child in the northern lane developed blackened swellings beneath the arms and died within two days. Soon after, her mother, two neighbors, and the priest’s servant fell ill. The symptoms described by the undertaker were terrifyingly swift: high fever, delirium, vomiting of blood, dark bruising across the chest and throat, and a smell “like meat kept too long in summer.” Those who showed signs of the disease rarely survived more than three days.

Once the scale of the outbreak became clear, the authorities ordered Fianaise Bhréagach sealed. Roads were blocked with carts, thorn hedges, and armed men. No one was permitted to leave. Food was left at a distance and collected only after the guards withdrew. Letters, if any were written, were burned rather than carried out. The villagers were told the quarantine would protect neighboring settlements, but the undertaker’s account suggests that, from the beginning, those outside the boundary expected no survivors.

The village collapsed with extraordinary speed. Families barricaded themselves indoors. The healthy abandoned the sick, then became sick themselves. Livestock wandered loose through the lanes. The church filled first with the dying, then with the dead, until the undertaker and the few men still able to stand could no longer move the bodies quickly enough. He writes of digging shallow trenches beyond the churchyard wall because consecrated ground had run out. He names entire households buried together, sometimes without certainty that all of them were dead.

Fear soon gave way to desperation. The account records mercy killings carried out by relatives, neighbors, and at least once by the undertaker himself. Some victims, raving and in agony, begged to be smothered before the swellings burst. Others were killed because their families believed death was inevitable and feared infection more than sin. The undertaker does not excuse these acts, but he records them with a numbness that suggests moral judgment had been overtaken by exhaustion. “God forgive us,” he writes in one fragment, “for we learned to call a pillow kindness.”

By the third week, no meaningful order remained. The priest was dead. The village headman was dead. The guards beyond the quarantine line no longer answered shouted pleas. Smoke rose from several houses that had been burned with bodies inside them. The undertaker describes dogs feeding in the street and bells tolling at irregular hours until the rope was cut down, either in anger or because no one could bear the sound. He continued to write names where he could, but as the deaths multiplied his record deteriorated into tallies, then marks, then unfinished sentences.

The final pages are the most fragmentary. They describe a mass burial in a pit near the western edge of the village, where dozens of bodies were laid in layers and covered with lime and soil. The undertaker believed he was among the last living inhabitants of Fianaise Bhréagach. He mentions one woman singing to a dead infant, a boy hiding beneath a cart, and a blind old man asking whether the quarantine had ended. There is no indication that any of them survived.

The undertaker’s own burial remains a mystery. He was not placed in the mass grave but hidden beneath the mortuary shed, suggesting that someone survived long enough to bury him separately, or that officials entered the village after the plague had burned itself out and chose to conceal his papers with his body. The position of the skeleton indicates a hurried burial. There was no coffin, no marker, and no sign of ceremony.

Most disturbing is what followed. The undertaker’s account implies that Fianaise Bhréagach was not merely abandoned but erased. Later administrative documents omit the village entirely. Land was redistributed without reference to its former inhabitants. The parish boundary was redrawn. Even the road leading into the settlement was allowed to vanish. Whether this erasure was intended to prevent panic, hide official cruelty, avoid claims of inheritance, or bury evidence of the failed quarantine remains uncertain.

The disease itself has never been conclusively identified. Some symptoms resemble bubonic or pneumonic plague, while others suggest hemorrhagic fever or an unknown epidemic illness. No single diagnosis accounts perfectly for the speed, mortality, and descriptions preserved in the manuscript. Because the site had been disturbed by centuries of weather, animal activity, and later agricultural use, biological evidence remains limited. What is clear is that the outbreak was nearly total. The village did not recover. It disappeared.

Today, the account of the Fianaise Bhréagach undertaker stands as a rare and unsettling testimony to a suppressed disaster. It is not a chronicle written by officials, physicians, or clergy, but by a man whose duty was to handle the dead until there were too many dead to handle. Through his fractured record, the village briefly reappears: its streets, its households, its terror, its final acts of mercy and violence. What had been removed from maps and memory returned from the ground, carried in the hands of the one man who had tried, until the end, to name the lost.

In September, the quiet village of Fianaise seemed to glow with a special kind of light. The mornings were cool, the fields were golden, and the first signs of autumn appeared along the narrow roads. People gathered in the town square to share stories, sell fresh produce, and enjoy the calm beauty of the changing season.

The name Fianaise meant “evidence,” and for many residents, the village itself was evidence of history, memory, and community. Old stone walls, weathered church bells, and handwritten letters kept in family homes all told the story of generations who had lived there before.

As September days grew shorter, Fianaise became a place of reflection. The people looked back on the warmth of summer while preparing for the colder months ahead. It was a time to remember, to gather, and to appreciate the simple signs of life all around them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark historical horror prose poem about a quarantined Irish village in 1607, framed by a modern discovery of an undertaker’s buried account, with archaic and grim imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
In the drought-split summer of 1998, when the bog gave back what it had swallowed, they found the little book beneath a rowan stump outside the ruined chapel of Cill Aodha.

It was wrapped in blackened calfskin, bound with a rosary gone green, and packed in salt as if it were meat for a voyage. The archaeologist who opened it said afterward that the pages exhaled like a mouth. Not dust, not mould, but a cold breath, wet and patient, smelling of peat smoke, grave wax, and old pennies.

On the first leaf, in a cramped hand browned by four centuries, was written:

**The Account of Muiris Ó Dálaigh, coffin-maker and layer-out of the dead, kept in the Year of Our Lord 1607, when the village was shut from the world by order of priest, captain, and fear.**

After that, no sermon. No mercy. Only tallies.

Three boards for Máire Ní Cinnéide, swollen in the throat.  
Two yards linen, though linen was wanting.  
One child wrapped with the mother, no name given.  
Nails saved and straightened from Seán the cooper’s shed.  
Payment: a silver brooch, cracked.

And then, as the pages passed under the lamp, the account began to loosen from numbers into confession.

We were sealed in at Michaelmas, when the oats stood black in the field and the crows would not peck them. The captain’s men drove stakes across the north road and hung red rags from ash poles, saying no soul was to pass beyond on pain of shot. The priest rang the bell till the rope bloodied his palms, then nailed the chapel door and spoke Mass through the shutter like a thief. Smoke stood low upon the thatches. Dogs went masterless. The well took on a taste of iron.

At first we named it fever, for fever is a common devil and sits often at Irish hearths. It came with blue lips, with eyes like skimmed milk, with a tongue blackened as if licked by the hearthstone. It made men call for wives buried twenty winters. It made women scratch scripture into their breasts. It made infants smile at corners where no nurse stood.

I had work in plenty.

The earth grew fat, but not deep enough.

I cut coffin planks by moonlight, for daylight was needed by the living to seek food in houses of the dead. My auger squealed like a hare in the snare. My mallet knew no Sabbath. I measured the poor with twine and the rich with the same twine. I shaved the dead men’s chins when their women begged it, though the razors dulled upon a bristle not altogether hair. I tied jaws shut with hemp. I weighted eyelids with farthings. Still they looked.

Still they looked.

In November, the graves began to mutter.

This I set down plain, though my hand rebels. There came from the churchyard after Compline a noise as of porridge boiling beneath turf. Not words at first, but a wet troubling, a pleading through clay. The widow Bríd ran there with a spade and was held by four men, biting them to the bone. “He is cold,” she cried. “My Eoghan is cold and calls for his cloak.”

But Eoghan had been buried with two cloaks, one wool and one sin.

The priest declared it vapours. The captain declared it sedition. I, who had placed them there, declared nothing.

By Advent the ground would not keep them.

The first to rise was little Peadar Ruadh, six years old, dead of the throat-swell and laid with hazel twigs across his breast. He came home at dawn, knocking softly as a polite child knocks, with clay packed in his ears and his small fingers worn to white sticks. His mother opened. We heard her singing before we heard her screaming.

When we broke the door, she had him on her lap and he had his face in the hollow of her neck, nursing where no milk lived.

After that, I was ordered not only to bury, but to bind. Stakes of yew through the winding sheet. Stones in the mouth. Thorn about the ankles. The priest gave me holy water; it steamed upon some and froze upon others. I set pennies under tongues for passage, but the ferryman would not have them. They came back with my coins green in their teeth.

No bell rang then. The rope hung stiff as a dead serpent.

Snow fell before Christmas, though the sky was clear. It fell upward from the graves.

A white dust rose from the churchyard in flakes and clung to the eaves. Children caught it on their tongues and died laughing. Old men crossed themselves with fingers that had no warmth. The hens laid eggs with shells soft as eyelids. In the byre, cattle turned their heads and spoke in the voices of drowned girls, naming names from before the English came, before the Normans, before Patrick, before Christ—old black names, bog-deep, stone-deep, names with roots in the marrow of the hill.

Then we knew the sickness was no sickness but a door.

And we had built our village atop the hinge.

The account falters there. Ink thickens, blots widen like flies. A thumbprint mars one margin, dark and reddish-brown, pressed so hard it broke the paper.

Yet Muiris continues.

On the Feast of St. Stephen, they brought me the priest.

He was not dead, though half his face had the look of a candle left too near flame. He begged me to make him a narrow box and nail it fast while he yet breathed.

“Undertaker,” said he, “there are mouths below us older than the sea, and we have fed them Christian flesh. They have learned our names.”

I told him no man should be buried living.

He laughed with no mirth and said, “Then bury me as something else.”

I did as he paid me. God forgive me. God turn His countenance away if He must.

We laid him under the altar, bound in chains taken from the captain’s stores, with salt, ash, and the Gospel of John upon his breast. He prayed until the clay covered him. Thereafter he barked. Thereafter he sang.

That night every grave in Cill Aodha opened like an eye.

They did not climb forth as corpses climb in tavern tales, stiff and foolish. They came as memories wearing meat. A husband with his wedding smile and no lower jaw. A babe trailing cord and grave-root. A girl dead of pox, lovely as May except for the beetles moving under her cheeks. They stood at every threshold, and each spoke in the voice most beloved by those within.

Open, a stór.  
Open, mother.  
Open, my heart, for the cold is upon me.  
Open, for I have forgiven thee.

Many opened.

By dawn, houses stood full and silent, their doors flapping in the wind like tongues.

I hid in my shed among planks and shrouds. Through a crack I saw the captain’s men flee for the north road. The red rags there had gone black. Beyond the stakes, something walked the boundary ditch: tall as a gallows, crowned in antlers, its hide a cloak of funeral linen stitched from many dead. It bent to each soldier as a lord bends to receive tribute, and where it touched them their armour filled with peat water and their screams became the cries of curlews.

No soul left Cill Aodha.

No soul, save perhaps this account, if paper may be a soul.

The last pages were found fused together. Conservators separated them with vapour and patience. Several lines are missing, eaten not by rot but by a round, deliberate burn, as if a small hot coin had rested there for centuries.

What remains is this:

I have buried all but myself.

I have put my wife beneath the crab-tree, though she asked me not to trouble, saying she would be up again before cockcrow. I have tied my sons together lest they wander lonely. I have filled the mouths of neighbours with salt until my hands split. I have no nails left. I have no prayers left. The dead stand outside and commend my workmanship.

They scratch at the door not to enter, but to be measured.

For below the chapel, beneath the priest, beneath the first bones of the first forgotten kings, there is an Undertaker older than I, and He keeps His account in darkness. Every coffin I made was a cradle for His hunger. Every grave was a letter addressed to Him. Every tolling bell a spoon upon His bowl.

He has sent for me now.

I hear my name spoken under the floorboards by mouths that never drew breath.

Muiris.  
Muiris Ó Dálaigh.  
Maker of boxes.  
Counter of dead.  
Come down and be counted.

The final entry is only a list.

One spade.  
One lantern.  
One length rope.  
One book, to be buried beneath rowan.  
One soul owing.

Payment: deferred.

The archaeologist who read this aloud did not finish his tea. By evening he complained of a taste of iron. By morning his tongue was dark. The excavation was sealed, the chapel fenced, the rowan stump removed to storage and later misplaced. Officially, the village of Cill Aodha never existed. No plague pit was recorded. No boundary stakes were found.

Yet in the photographs taken that first day, before the rain came, there are marks in the mud around the trench: small footprints, bare and inward-facing, as if a crowd of children had stood watching the book unearthed from below.

And on the inside cover, unnoticed until the scan was enlarged, another hand had written beneath Muiris’s name—fresher, darker, the ink not yet wholly dry:

**Account reopened, 1998.**

counterfactuals.output:
## From the Box Marked *Fianaise Bhréagach*  
### A reconstructed found-document account, translated and arranged from damaged parish papers, private memoranda, and one undertaker’s deposition

No village by the name of **Fianaise Bhréagach** appears on the modern surveys.

Its absence is not unusual in itself. Villages are abandoned, renamed, folded into estates, or swallowed by roads. What is unusual is the thoroughness of the omission. The tithe maps jump over the valley where it is supposed to have stood. Parish registers for the relevant years are missing, but only those years. The county mortality returns for the district contain three blank pages, ruled and headed, then left empty. In the index of burials there is a torn place between *Fiachra’s Well* and *Finlan’s Acre*, the paper scraped so hard that lamplight shines through it.

Yet the village was real.

Its name survives in three places: an invoice for lime, a letter from a magistrate asking that “the matter of Fianaise Bhréagach be kept from needless repetition,” and a nailed cedar box discovered in the loft of the abandoned courthouse at Cill Dara in 1891. Inside the box were twenty-seven loose pages, a broken rosary, a child’s shoe hardened with black mud, and the testimony of one **Seán Ó Dálaigh**, undertaker.

The following account is taken chiefly from Ó Dálaigh’s statement. The spelling of names has been regularized where possible. Blots, tears, and illegible passages are marked only where they affect the sense.

No official inquiry is known to have followed. No memorial stone has been found.

---

## The Testimony of Seán Ó Dálaigh, Undertaker  
*Given, by his own hand, “in the winter after the white cough,” and found among sealed papers*

I write this not to clear my name, for there is no name left in Fianaise Bhréagach to accuse me, but because I was the last man there whose trade required him to count.

A priest counts sins. A doctor counts pulses. An undertaker counts bodies.

By that measure, I knew the village more truly than any living man.

Fianaise Bhréagach lay in a low green hollow between two hills, with a road through it like a grey thread and the church above it, looking down. There were forty-one houses if one counted widow Mairéad’s lean-to behind the forge, which I always did, because she paid rent on the patch and had a door of her own. There were three wells, one blessed, one brackish, and one that went dry in August. There were two hundred and six souls by the priest’s last reckoning before the sickness came.

I had buried most of their fathers.

I had coffined infants no longer than my forearm and old men who seemed already made of turf. I had set hinges on boxes for girls in their wedding year, and I had planed pine smooth for men taken by horse-kick, fever, knife, and winter. Death was no stranger to me. It came to the village often enough, but always as a visitor. It sat at one hearth, then another, and left by morning.

This time it came to stay.

The first was Nóra Bhailís, wife to the miller.

That is how I remember it, though others, while there were others to argue, said the first was a travelling peddler who slept in the hayloft at Ó hAodha’s farm and left before dawn, coughing into a rag. But no man saw him die, and I am speaking of deaths.

Nóra was thirty-two years of age, broad-shouldered, red-handed from flour and water, and stronger than her husband. She took ill on a Tuesday. Her tongue turned dark. Her eyes watered as if she had been standing in smoke. By evening she had a cough that did not sound to be coming from the lungs, but from something lower, deeper, as if the grave itself had got hold of a string inside her and was pulling.

I was sent for on Thursday.

When I entered the mill house, the air had a sweet, wet smell, like apples left too long under straw. Nóra lay uncovered though the day was cold. Her skin was white except around the mouth, where it had gone a bruised blue. There were little black beads at the corners of her lips. Not blood. Not phlegm. Something thicker.

Her husband said, “Make it quick, Seán. For the children’s sake.”

I asked where the children were.

He pointed to the loft.

I heard them coughing above us.

By Saturday they were all in boxes: Nóra, her husband Tomás, their daughters Bríd and Caitlín, and the small boy whose name I shamefully cannot put down, though I made his coffin from the last clean board in my shed. The priest, Father Eoghan, came to bless them. He would not step inside the house. He stood at the threshold with his stole over his mouth and spoke the words too quickly.

We buried them at the north wall because the family plot was full.

That was the last proper funeral in Fianaise Bhréagach.

After that, there was no time for ceremony.

The sickness moved house to house, but not like fire, which follows thatch and wind. It chose strangely. It took the blacksmith and spared the apprentice sleeping beside him. It took every child in the schoolmaster’s cottage but left the schoolmaster himself alive for nine days, walking from room to room with his slate under his arm, writing names in chalk on doors so I would know who lay within.

The marks of it were these:

First, a watering of the eyes.

Second, a taste of metal in the mouth, so the sufferers said.

Third, a cough, soft at first, almost polite.

Fourth, a whitening of the skin and a darkening at the lips and nails.

Fifth, the black beads.

After the beads appeared, no one lasted more than a day.

The doctor came from Baile an Chnoic on the second week, sent by the magistrate. He was a young man with yellow gloves and a horse that would not drink from our stream. He examined three patients, burned his handkerchief, and told us to boil water, burn bedding, and keep apart.

Keep apart.

He might as well have told the rain not to wet us.

We had one road, one church, one forge, one mill, and one fear. People gathered despite themselves. They gathered at wells. They gathered at the churchyard. They gathered outside my door asking how many boards I had left, how much lime, how deep a grave should be if there were four in it, whether a body could be wrapped in a sheet if no coffin could be had, whether God would know the difference.

I told them God would know His own.

I do not know if I believed it. But I said it because they needed an answer, and because an undertaker who cannot speak comfort is only a carpenter with a shovel.

By the seventeenth day, I had no coffins.

I had used pine, oak, old doors, a tabletop, two shutters from the schoolhouse, and the sideboards of Father Eoghan’s own bed. I had buried thirteen without boxes, wrapped in linen and sacking. I had stopped measuring. I dug trenches beyond the east wall of the graveyard because consecrated ground had filled. Father Eoghan objected at first. Then he developed the cough.

He confessed himself aloud in the church with no one near him. His voice carried through the closed door. I was in the yard with my spade and heard him say he had doubted God’s mercy. Then he laughed, once, and begged pardon for laughing.

When I found him the next morning, he was lying before the altar with his hands folded properly, as if he had arranged himself before dying. There were black beads on the altar cloth.

I buried him alone.

I used no bell. The bell rope had been cut down for bindings.

By then we had begun to burn houses.

This was ordered by the magistrate’s men, who came no farther than the old bridge. They shouted instructions across the water and left sacks of lime, vinegar, and three loaves. One of them read from a paper that all contaminated dwellings were to be put to flame after removal of the dead.

Removal of the dead.

Those words do not bend under the weight they are made to carry.

I removed the dead from Ó hAodha’s farm with a scarf tied around my nose and mouth and my hands wrapped in rags soaked in vinegar. In the bed were the mother and two sons. In the pantry was the grandmother, seated upright beside a crock of butter. In the loft, where the peddler was said to have slept, I found no body, only a dark stain on the hay and a pack of cheap ribbons, combs, and little mirrors.

I kept one mirror. I do not know why. Perhaps because I wanted proof that faces still existed.

When we burned the farm, the cattle lowed in the fields until dark.

On the twenty-fourth day, the village no longer sounded like a village.

No hammer. No cart. No children. No geese shrieking in the lane. Only coughing, when the wind was right, and the crack of burning beams.

Those still unstruck avoided one another’s eyes. To look at a man was to wonder how deep he would have to be buried. To look at a woman was to imagine lifting her by the shoulders when she could no longer stand. Shame came into all our dealings. We became embarrassed before death, as if the dying had committed some indecency by doing it where we could see.

My wife, Sorcha, had begged me to leave.

She was not from Fianaise Bhréagach. She had people westward, beyond the bog road. We had no children living. She said there was nothing holding us but graves, and graves did not care who dug them.

I told her I could not go.

She asked whether I had married the village or her.

I had no answer that did not condemn me.

She left on a Monday morning with a shawl over her hair and my mother’s silver pin at her throat. I watched her take the western road. She did not turn back, which I resented then and admired later. For three days I believed her saved.

On the fourth day, I found her sitting under the ash tree by Tobar Naomh, the blessed well, too weak to walk farther. Her lips were blue.

She said, “You see, Seán? I did leave.”

I carried her home.

I had made coffins for every soul in that valley who could pay me and many who could not, but I had never made one for Sorcha. While she slept, I went to the shed and chose the best boards left, though they were warped and smoke-stained. My hands shook so badly I split the first plank driving a nail. I cursed the nail, the plank, myself, and God, in that order.

She died before dawn.

There were no black beads on her mouth.

I remember being grateful for that, as if dignity had been spared her.

I buried her beside our sons.

After Sorcha, my counting changed. I no longer counted the dead. I counted the living.

Thirty-one.

Then twenty-eight.

Then twenty.

Then eleven.

By the time the soldiers came, there were seven of us able to stand: myself, the schoolmaster, blind Peadar, the widow Mairéad, young Ailbhe from the forge, a farmhand called Cormac, and little Róisín Ní Chathasaigh, who had survived in a cupboard for two days after her mother died against the door.

The soldiers wore cloth over their faces and would not enter the houses. Their captain informed us that the village was under seal. No one was to depart. Food would be left at the bridge. The dead were to be burned where burial was not possible.

The schoolmaster asked by what law.

The captain said, “By necessity.”

The schoolmaster said he would write that down.

He was dead that evening.

It is a terrible thing to become accustomed to horror. Worse still is to become practical with it. I learned which doors to break first. I learned to wrap the dead tightly so limbs would not fall loose. I learned that a shallow grave for a child takes less time than weeping, and so the weeping must wait. I learned to drink nothing I had not boiled and to eat standing up. I learned not to pray over every body, because the living needed my breath more than the dead did.

Then blind Peadar began ringing the church bell.

How he climbed the tower I do not know. The rope had been cut, as I said, but he must have found the stump of it. The bell sounded at midnight, not in tolls but in wild, uneven blows, as if the church itself were coughing iron.

I went to fetch him down.

He was in the bell chamber with blood on his hands from pulling the frayed rope. He asked if the road was full.

“What road?” I said.

“The road out,” he said. “I hear them all walking.”

There was no one walking. The village below lay black and still, with only two house-fires glowing.

Peadar smiled toward the sound of my breathing.

“They don’t know they’re dead,” he said.

He died before morning.

I do not say I saw ghosts. Let no man put that in my mouth. I say only that when a place is filled with the unburied, the mind peoples the dark.

On the thirty-ninth day, the widow Mairéad and Cormac tried to cross the bridge.

I did not stop them. Had Sorcha been alive, I might have gone too.

The soldiers fired warning shots. Cormac ran anyway. He fell before reaching the far bank. Whether struck by a ball or by weakness, I cannot say. Mairéad stood in the road screaming that she was not sick, that she had washed herself in vinegar, that she would sleep in a ditch and speak to no one. A soldier knocked her down with the butt of his musket.

They left her on our side.

She spat blood by sunset.

I buried her with Cormac two days later, after the captain allowed me to retrieve his body. The captain apologized from behind his cloth mask. I remember that clearly. He said, “I am sorry for it.”

I asked him which part.

He did not answer.

By then little Róisín had stopped speaking. She followed me everywhere, holding a strip of my coat. I gave her broth. I told her stories badly. At night she slept in Sorcha’s chair. Once, I woke and found her standing over me, touching my face to see if I was warm.

Ailbhe from the forge lasted longest of all besides me. She was seventeen, maybe eighteen, with cropped hair and arms corded from hammer work. She helped me dig when she had strength. She did not cry until we found the bodies in the chapel cellar.

I had not known they were there.

Some had hidden below the chapel when the burning began, thinking stone would protect them. There were nine in all. The air that came out when we opened the cellar door drove us both back into the yard.

Ailbhe sat on a grave marker and put her fists against her eyes.

“There’ll be no one to say we were here,” she said.

I told her I was writing names.

This was a lie. I had stopped writing names because there were too many and because my hands were always dirty.

She said, “Write mine first, then.”

So I did.

**Ailbhe Ní Fheargail. Forge. Living.**

She laughed when she saw the word living.

Three days later I crossed it out.

After that it was only Róisín and me.

I thought, in my foolishness, that perhaps the sickness had passed us by. Perhaps God, having taken His tithe, had left the gleanings.

I washed the child’s face every morning. I combed her hair with a peddler’s comb I had found in Ó hAodha’s loft. I made her recite the names of birds so she would use her voice: rook, wren, thrush, lark.

On the forty-seventh day, her eyes began to water.

I will not write much of this.

She was six years old.

She asked if her mother was angry that she had hidden in the cupboard.

I said no.

She asked if I would put her in the ground or the fire.

I said the ground.

She asked if it would be dark.

I said yes, but only like sleep.

She considered this, then asked whether I could leave the lid a little open.

There are requests a man cannot grant and cannot refuse. I told her I would see what could be done.

She died near dawn, holding the broken rosary from the box in which these papers were found. I had given it to her because she liked the feel of the beads.

I made her coffin from the last of the church pews.

I did not leave the lid open.

Forgive me.

When the soldiers returned in force, they found me in the graveyard. I had dug but not filled her grave. I was sitting beside it with the spade across my knees. The captain asked how many remained.

I said, “One.”

He looked around and asked where the child was.

I said, “None.”

They burned the rest of the village over the next two days: mill, forge, schoolhouse, cottages, chapel roof, my own home, my shed, and all the records they found in Father Eoghan’s press. The captain said it was for public safety. Papers carry sickness, he said.

Perhaps they do. But I saw him set aside some pages before the burning. Registers. Lists. Letters. He gave them to a clerk, who sealed them in oilcloth.

I asked why those were spared.

He said, “So that the necessary facts may be preserved.”

I asked whether our names were necessary.

He did not answer.

Before they took me away, I walked once through the village street. There was no street left, only chimneys and hot stone. The blessed well had been filled with lime. The church bell had cracked from heat and lay in the nave like a great black tongue.

At the bridge, I turned back.

Smoke covered the hollow so completely that Fianaise Bhréagach seemed already erased, not ruined but rubbed out.

The clerk asked me to state the final number for the record.

I told him two hundred and five dead.

He said the priest’s last count was two hundred and six.

I said, “I am not dead.”

He looked at me for a long while and wrote something different.

I saw it.

He wrote: **No survivors.**

That is why I make this testimony now. Not for justice. Justice has no road into that valley. Not for remembrance, though God knows the dead deserve it. I write because a lie was entered where my life should have been.

If these pages are found, let it be known:

There was a village called Fianaise Bhréagach.

It had a mill and a forge and three wells. It had children who knew the names of birds. It had a priest who doubted and prayed anyway. It had a woman named Sorcha who tried to live. It had a girl named Ailbhe who asked to be written down. It had a child named Róisín who wanted the dark left open.

I, Seán Ó Dálaigh, undertaker, counted them.

I carried them.

I buried what I could.

And I was there.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak narrative poem about a 17th-century disease outbreak in an isolated village, featuring a messenger horse, sentries, villagers dying, and an undertaker forced to bury everyone.
counterfactuals.output:
In the year of our Lord, when the frost would not thaw,  
and the black pines leaned like judges over snow,  
there lay a village beyond the marsh and moor,  
with one road in and none where a soul might go.  

At dawn the bell was muffled with a rag,  
for even bronze seemed frightened of the air;  
the baker’s boy lay blue beneath his sack,  
the miller coughed blood into his prayer.  

They barred the lane with cartwheel, chain, and spear;  
two sentries stood where the last bridge thinned—  
one with a matchlock, one with a psalm,  
both turning pale in the fever-wind.  

No wagons came with grain or salt,  
no priest rode up with book and flame;  
only a messenger horse at dusk,  
foam-lipped, riderless, blood on its mane.  

It stamped before the plague-marked gate,  
its saddle split, its satchel torn;  
inside, a writ from the magistrate:  
*No man shall pass till none are born.*  

The sentries read it by lantern-smoke,  
then crossed themselves and looked away;  
behind the hedge the mothers cried,  
and children dwindled into clay.  

The sickness moved from cot to cot,  
a guest that knocked with knuckled bone;  
it supped at every wooden board  
and slept where husbands slept alone.  

The blacksmith’s fire was left to ash,  
the school slate froze beneath the rhyme;  
hens went unfed in shuttered yards,  
and dogs howled thin against the lime.  

One man remained to dig the earth—  
Old Enoch Graye, with spade and cord,  
the undertaker, stooped and gaunt,  
who cursed both king and living Lord.  

He measured not with ribbon now,  
nor planed the coffins smooth and square;  
he wrapped them in their marriage sheets  
and dragged them by their yellow hair.  

At first he set them two by two,  
with names cut deep in alder pegs;  
by week’s end names had lost their use,  
and he buried arms apart from legs.  

He buried the sexton by the bell,  
the midwife under the frozen sty,  
the sentry who had dropped his gun,  
and the other who would not die—  

who begged beyond the barricade,  
his face a lantern, green with breath;  
but orders nailed the village shut,  
and mercy was another death.  

So Enoch dug through root and stone,  
through Sabbath, storm, and moonless rain;  
the messenger horse stood at the gate,  
still waiting, shivering in its chain.  

It watched him fill the parish field,  
then orchard, ditch, and cattle shed;  
it watched the houses fall to hush,  
their hearths gone cold, their windows dead.  

At last no crying crossed the roofs,  
no cough, no hymn, no cradle’s creak;  
only the spade in Enoch’s hands  
and snow collecting on his cheek.  

He dug one grave beneath the yew,  
a narrow bed, but long and deep;  
he laid the final infant there,  
too light to trouble even sleep.  

Then stood he by the messenger horse,  
and read the writ once more by dawn;  
the ink had bled, the seal had cracked,  
the king’s own name was almost gone.  

“None shall pass till none remain,”  
he said, and laughed without a sound;  
then took the beast beyond the posts,  
and led it through the burial ground.  

The sentries’ bones kept watch no more,  
the bridge lay white, the marsh lay wide;  
but Enoch stopped at the village edge  
and turned back inward, hollow-eyed.  

For who would bury the burying man,  
when plague had eaten kin and kin?  
He dug beside the common pit,  
then calmly climbed and lay therein.  

The horse went on through fog and thorn,  
with empty reins and lowered head;  
at every town its hoofbeats warned  
what law had made among the dead.  

And far behind, where the black pines lean,  
the village sank without a name—  
no smoke, no bell, no witness left,  
but graves and snow and a horse’s shame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an atmospheric folk-horror passage set in September 1607 about a village destroyed by an unknown illness, written as if recovered centuries later from a hidden manuscript.
counterfactuals.output:
**From a paper bundle found behind the wainscot of the former rectory at H—, during repairs in 1894; the hand appears early seventeenth century, much stained by damp. The following lines are legible.**

September, in the Year of Our Lord 1607.

I set these words down not for any living man of this parish, for there are few such remaining, but that some eye hereafter may know we were once called by names, and had hearths, and sowed rye upon the west field, and rang the bell at Michaelmas.

The sickness came first with the turning of the leaves, when the hedgerows were black with sloes and the air smelt of apples fallen soft in the grass. It did not enter as plague enters, with swellings under the arm and groin, nor as the sweating sickness, swift and hot as a coal. It came quietly. Men rose from their beds saying they had dreamt all night of bells under water. By noon their tongues were dark. By evening they could not bear the sight of iron, nor the sound of prayer.

Old Mother Ede, who knew simples and birth-charms, said it was no Christian fever. She found in the throats of the dead a greenish stain, like moss upon a stone, and beneath the nails a black earth though none had dug. The children were taken next. They stood at the edge of the common in their linen shifts and answered when no one called them. When their mothers went to fetch them in, they said there was a man among the elder trees, crowned with a nest of thorns, who promised them warm bread.

On the seventh day no cock crew.

On the ninth day the mill stopped, though the stream ran full.

On the twelfth day we carried six to the pit beyond the churchyard, for consecrated ground was already broken and heaped past decency. We had no boards left for coffins, and so wrapped them in sheets. Yet when we lowered them down, the earth shuddered beneath the ropes, and from the hole came a smell not of rot, but of green things bruised in spring.

Master Vey, the rector, bade us fast and confess. He preached with a cloth tied over his mouth, his eyes watering, his hands shaking upon the pulpit. “The Lord hath turned His face,” he cried, “for some sin hidden among us.” At that, Joan Pike laughed, though her husband lay dead across their threshold. She laughed until blood ran from her nose and said, “Not hidden. Buried.”

Afterward they searched the old barrow on Cresset Hill.

I was not among the diggers, being weak by then, yet I saw them go with spades, mattocks, and two lanterns though it was full day. They found, as was told me, no bones of Saxon king nor Dane, but a door of oak under the chalk, bound in blackened hoops, without hinge or handle. Upon it were cut marks like no letters I have seen, save that they made the eye unwilling to rest on them. Thomas Mere struck it once with his pick, and all the sheep in the lower pasture began screaming like women.

That night the village did not sleep.

There was knocking from beneath every floor.

At dawn the well was found choked with leaves, though none had fallen near it; and in each leaf was writ, in a small red hand, the name of one yet living.

By then the houses stood open, for who had strength to bar them? Smoke went cold in the chimneys. The lanes were full of straw from sickbeds and bowls of untouched broth. I saw no dogs. I saw no birds. Only the flies remained, fat and bright as beads, gathered thick upon the church windows where they crawled in the shape of words.

I will not write what became of the rector. God forgive him if he acted from terror. God forgive us that we let him.

This morning, the twenty-third of September, I walked as far as the green. The mist lay low, and through it I perceived figures moving from house to house. Not thieves, nor neighbours, for their limbs were too long and they bent their heads beneath no lintel. Where they passed, the thatch sweated and the walls darkened with mould. One came to the door of my house and stood without. It wore my father’s voice and asked to be let in.

I have dragged the chest across the door.

My wife breathes no more. Little Anne has ceased her singing.

There is a bell ringing now, though the rope was cut yesterday and the tower stands empty.

If any soul find this paper, pray not for us by name. Speak no name written here aloud. Cover the well. Burn the elder trees. Let the hill alone.

For the illness was not an illness, but an asking.

And we, being hungry, answered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a macabre historical ballad in first person from the perspective of a village undertaker during a plague quarantine, with references to burning a horse, dying children, and mass graves.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Undertaker’s Quarantine Ballad**

I am the man with the tar-black cart,  
With a bell that will not sing;  
I pass where the shuttered cottages start  
At the scrape of an iron ring.  
No priest walks out, no mother cries—  
They’ve nailed the chapel door—  
And the red cross blooms where a household dies,  
Then blooms on twenty more.

The road to town is choked with thorn,  
The watchmen keep the gate;  
No loaf comes in with the waking morn,  
No letter outruns fate.  
The alderman called from ten yards wide,  
“Take coin, and do not fail—  
But dig them deep on the moorland side,  
And cover them under shale.”

So I take the small, and I take the old,  
And I take the bride in lace;  
I take the strong men stiff and cold,  
With terror still in the face.  
I have wrapped dead children in winding sheets  
Too short for a full-grown prayer;  
Their little shoes sit in the empty streets,  
And no one is left to care.

The surgeon fled by the river path,  
The sexton drank and died;  
The baker’s boy, with a blistered wrath,  
Was buried at eventide.  
The schoolhouse hums with flies by noon,  
The well gives a bitter breath;  
And every cradle, still as the moon,  
Has rocked itself to death.

Our plough horse, Brindle, broke his trace  
And staggered through the square;  
Foam on his lips, and a glassy gaze,  
And plague-smoke in his hair.  
They said the beast had carried doom  
From farm to farm that week;  
We burned him down by the lime-kiln gloom  
Till the hide began to reek.

I watched the mane catch blue, then red,  
I heard the sinews snap;  
The children peered from a fever-bed  
Through many a shutter gap.  
“Go in,” I said, “for the ash is foul,”  
But their eyes were bright with pain;  
By dawn I bore them, cowl by cowl,  
Through the same grey lane.

No churchyard keeps what we have become—  
Its stones are overrun;  
So I dig where the heath lies deaf and dumb  
And the curlew shuns the sun.  
The mass graves gape like a hungry choir,  
Wide-mouthed, rank, and raw;  
I lower them in by the lantern fire,  
Without a name or law.

There’s Mistress Vale with her silver comb,  
There’s Tom who mended shoes;  
There’s half the inn and half my home,  
And all the miller’s ewes.  
I stack them close, for the pit is wide,  
Yet never wide enough;  
The earth falls soft on the groom and bride,  
On velvet, rags, and rough.

I do not weep; I’ve forgotten how,  
My tears are lime and clay.  
I only lift, and bind, and bow,  
And cart the night away.  
But sometimes under the death-bell’s tone,  
When the plague wind crawls in slow,  
I think I hear my own name groan  
From the trench below.

My wife wore blue on Whitsun last;  
My son chased rooks in spring.  
I buried them both when the frost bit fast,  
And kept my iron ring.  
The parish paid me in bread gone green,  
In candles, salt, and thread;  
And I, who walk where life has been,  
Am servant to the dead.

So bar your doors, you living few,  
And breathe through cloth and fear;  
The cart comes round when the rash comes blue,  
And I shall soon be near.  
For plague is lord of field and fen,  
Of cradle, crown, and spade—  
And I am the last of honest men  
Who plies an honest trade.
